The MSS. from which this edition has been prepared, .are 
these: — 
1. A - the Copenhagen MS. No. VI (Singh. character). F = C aeu `. 
2. M — the Phayre MS. of the India Office Library WA n"

— t was my purpose to do equal justice to the Singhalese 
and the Burmese tradition. I was not unaware, from texts 
_edited by Childers and other scholars, that the Birmans are far 
more conscientious in transcribing canonical writings. than the 
/ Ə experience derived from Milindapaüha and the Jātaka prose 
might lead us to infer. The collation proved that M® on the 
wholeagrees pretty closely with A, and further, that in some 
_ instances it has preserved the original reading with greater 
fidelity than the MSS. of Ceylon, as far as I can judge from 
Zy the Copenhagen collection. Thus, the following Burmese 
readings are certainly preferable to those of the Singh. MSS.: — 
lokānukampāya p.21, 1. 27; patbamam jhānam, etc. p. 21, 1. 36; 
_acchodakā, etc. p. 76, 1. 27; dhūmāyati p. 142, 1. 20; vilahgakena 
p. 207,1. 22; yavad- e p. 207,1. 31; upapajjati in certain phrases. 
"Lo Also the spellings nikujjati p. 24, 1. 3, saminjati p. 57, 1. 7, vam- 
~ bheti p. 19, 1. 3, are better than nikkujjeti, sammiüjati, vamheti, 
as the Singhalese write almost always. 
..In other cases the Burmese readings are much on a par 
with the Singhalese, as, aranüavanapatthàni p. 16, 1. 29 (perhaps

M properly speaking represents two texts, the transcriber's 


(Ma) and the corrector's (Mb). The latter was no very bad 


Zo scholar, and without his amendments the MS. would have been 


of much less value. Ma, for instance, never adds anusvāra to 
-i, frequently confounds -i -i and -u -ū, and commits all the

— A and M occasionally agree in errors: — vivattayi p. 12,1. 5,

/ <  Buddhaghosa's commentary has been of very great service. 
Whenever his readings, from his comments upon them, are unmis- 
takable, they must in my opinion be adopted in spite of other 
, authorities. His MSS, were at least fifteen centuries older than 
ours, and in a first edition we certainly cannot aim at anything 
/s"higher than reproducing his text as far as possible.! The Copen- 
— — hagen MS. (C) seems to be tolerably correct; only a most in- 
competent corrector has been at work in a considerable portion 
of it, and though his blunders are easily detected, the circum- 
stance tends to render the corrections of that MS. generally 
"Lo speaking doubtful I have often followed C, where A and M 
7 A differed, and its readings are sometimes right in spite of their 
authority; cf. udabindu p. 78, 1. 34, nati p. 115, 1. 22, adhigacche 
p. 275, 1. 16, etc. 
- | have often and with great advantage consulted numerous 
z«—parallels, both passages of some length, as p. 163 gt seq., p. 240 
et seq., etc., and shorter phrases recurring either in the same 
Nikāya or in the other three. Some caution in using them is. 
however, necessary. In the first place, it does happen that the 
parallels favour a reading very little acceptable, and that the 
3 o true form is only found at one place or in a minority of sources. 
^ A Comp. n. on tatiyo, catuttho p. 48, 1. 6, (samāpanna p. 72, 1. 267), 
„ajinam p. 78, 1. 12, tam -eva p. 80, 1.30.. Cf. also n. on p. 166, 
|. 13. Secondly, it must be admitted that in all probability there 


are real discrepancies between the different Nikayas — occa-

The Lalita-Vistara abounds in parallels, but they are 
Z not available in fixing the readings of our text, unless it be at 
p.481, 1. 2 and very few other places. 
I have met with a few quotations, which, though they have

degree, to corroborate a dubious or difficult reading, or have
